newsitem.title: UK: Britons win case against Hoover on free flights.
newsitem.headline: Britons win case against Hoover on free flights.

text.p: A British judge ruled on Friday that U.S. appliance giant Hoover should have provided free flights for two customers who bought vacuum cleaners to quality for a controversial promotional scheme in 1994.
The ruling was the latest in a long line of court defeats for Hoover over its hugely over-subscribed flight offer, one of the most disastrous promotional campaigns in corporate history.
Several senior executives were sacked and Hoover had to spend millions of pounds to cover the cost of the air fares.
An estimated 300,000 people took part. Customers who spent more than 100 pounds on a Hoover appliance could apply for two free flights to the United States or continental Europe.
But thousands complained that Hoover imposed new conditions, offered inconvenient flights or mysteriously lost applications.
Judge Ivor Bennett of St Helens County Court in northwest England said Hoover should have provided free flights even if households had sent in more than one application.
Hoover had argued there had been a special clause in the promotion restricting households to just one application and this invalidated all multiple claims made.
But Bennett ruled this meant each household could only get two free flights, not that they should miss out altogether.

The case was bought by Peter Lucas of Sutton Coldfield, northern England and Norman Magowan of Belfast, who said they should both have qualified for two free tickets even though Lucas' son and Magowan's wife had sent in separate applications.

The cases are the first in a series of 20 coordinated actions being fought in St Helens by lawyer Nick Davies. He has thousands of other clients in a "class action" hoping to win compensation from Hoover if the test cases are successful.
"It's a great result. But this is only part of the battle," said Davies. No one from Hoover was available for comment.
Damages, expected to be in the region of 1,000 pounds ($1,621), will be assessed next week.
